$comment: Per-suite pixel tolerances against the LibreOffice oracle.
`maxDiffRatio` is the fraction of pixels allowed to differ by more than
`threshold` (pixelmatch's 0..1 perceptual distance). Every tolerance has a written
reason. Widening one is a decision to record here, not a knob to turn quietly — if a
diff grows, the first question is whether the viewer regressed, and the second is
whether the oracle is the thing that is wrong.
The oracle is LibreOffice, not PowerPoint. It antialiases differently, hints text
differently, and rasterises effects differently, so a tolerance of zero is not
achievable for anything with text in it. For the milestones where fidelity matters
most (m2, m4), keep PowerPoint-exported references for manual spot checks.

suites.reason: A blank slide is flat white. Anything above noise here is a real bug.
suites.scoreAsReason: A blank slide. Any engine scoring above noise here is broken.

suites.reason: One text box and one rectangle. The rectangle should be near-exact; the tolerance is almost entirely the text's antialiasing and hinting.
suites.scoreAsReason: One textbox and one rectangle; the diff is dominated by the glyphs.

suites.reason: Text-heavy by design. LibreOffice's line breaking and glyph rasterisation differ from a browser's even when the wrap points agree, and a single word moving to another line lights up a large fraction of the slide. Watch the trend, not the absolute number; check wrap points via debugTrace when it moves.

Preset geometry. This sat at 3.5% while hiding four real bugs — a star5 whose waist was halved, a hexagon that missed the top and bottom of its box, can and cube drawing their lit faces as white holes, and arrowheads scaled by the shape's width instead of its shorter side. All four were plainly wrong to the eye and none moved the number past a third of the old budget, which is the lesson: on a suite of small shapes on a large slide, a loose tolerance is not a safety margin, it is a blindfold. Now 0.03-0.28% across the three slides, so 0.6% is roughly double the worst and leaves room for antialiasing along curved edges without leaving room for a shape to be the wrong shape. Look at the diff image when this moves; a geometry error is obvious there and invisible here.

The inheritance suite: every shape takes its position, size and formatting from the layout and master. Text dominates the diff, so the tolerance matches m2. A *positional* error would blow well past this, which is exactly what this suite is for.
suites.scoreAsReason: Inheritance, but the visible diff is nearly all body text.

suites.reason: Table borders land on half-pixel boundaries and LibreOffice snaps them differently, so every rule contributes a line of differing pixels. Cell text carries the rest.
suites.scoreAsReason: Table rules, fills and banding dominate over the cell text.

suites.reason: Deliberately the loosest suite. chart.xml carries data and formatting but no geometry, so every renderer computes the plot itself: LibreOffice picks its own axis scale, gap widths, label placement and legend metrics, and none of those are specified by the file. The structural things this suite actually guards are that the right number of bars/wedges appear, in the right order, with distinct series colours, inside the frame — a regression in any of those blows well past this figure. Judge it by the trend and by looking at the diff, not by the number alone.
suites.scoreAsReason: chart.xml carries no geometry, so every renderer invents its own axis scale, gap widths and label placement. Scoring that compares arbitrary choices.

suites.reason: Gradients, alpha compositing and the outer shadow all render, and this suite now sits near 0.1%. The remaining budget is for the Gaussian blur radius, which LibreOffice and a browser compute differently — matching it exactly would mean matching its implementation. Note what this tolerance can and cannot catch: an effect vanishing entirely only moves the figure by about half a percent, so the real guard against that is the unit tests in layout::tests, which assert the SetShadow command and its scope directly. Pixel tolerance is the wrong instrument for 'did this feature stop working'.

A gradient-filled title on a dark background. The fixture exists because a gradient on text was being anchored to the slide origin rather than to the glyphs, so the title rendered one flat colour. Large-point bold text on a dark ground is the worst case for antialiasing differences — every glyph edge contributes — which is what the budget is for. What it guards is that the colour *varies* across the title; a regression to a flat fill moves the figure well past this.
suites.scoreAsReason: A gradient-filled title: text, and little else.

suites.reason: Preset hatch fills, as a slide background and as a shape fill. Both previously collapsed to a flat blended colour. LibreOffice draws preset hatches faithfully, so this is a real oracle comparison. The budget is for tile phase: the repeat is quantised to the device grid, so a sub-pixel difference in where the pattern starts shifts every stripe on the slide and lights up a large fraction of it while looking identical to the eye. A hatch regressing to a flat fill blows well past this.

Tiled bitmap fills, deliberately NOT compared against the oracle. LibreOffice ignores <a:tile> and stretches the image to fill the shape — the exact bug this fixture exists to catch. Diffing against it would invert the test: a correct repeating render scores ~4% while a regression back to stretching would score near zero, so the suite would pass loudest when the feature was broken. It compares against a reviewed reference instead, which catches regressions without pretending to verify fidelity. Fidelity here is argued from the spec and asserted in layout::paint::tests (scale and offset survive into the display list) — and the tolerance is tight because our own output should be deterministic.
suites.scoreAsReason: LibreOffice ignores <a:tile> and stretches the image, so an engine that tiles correctly scores worse than one that repeats the oracle's bug. Scoring this rewards being wrong.
Twenty-nine flowchart presets and no text at all.
suites.reason: The flowchart family, all 29 of it. This fixture exists because a capability diff against @aiden0z/pptx-renderer found 22 of these falling back to their bounding rectangle, and nothing in the suite noticed. Now 1.24%, down from 2.16% after five curves were corrected against sampled reference profiles: terminator was a stadium where the spec gives elliptical caps at 0.161w, inputOutput scaled its slant by the shorter side where the spec says the width, document's bottom wave was symmetric where the real one is not, and punchedTape and multidocument both had the wrong wave. Three of those five — terminator, inputOutput and document — shipped in M1 and were wrong for as long as they had existed; nothing covered them. The budget is close to the figure on purpose: these are flat polygons and arcs with no text, so a move here means a shape changed shape.

suites.scoreAsReason: LibreOffice draws action buttons flat, so it cannot adjudicate the bevel.
suites.reason: The twelve action buttons. NOT compared against the oracle, for the same reason as m5f: LibreOffice renders these as flat rectangles with no bevel at all, while PowerPoint draws them raised and the preset's own pathLst carries lightenLess and darkenLess faces to do it. Diffing against LibreOffice would score the bevel as error and reward removing it — the blank button alone, which has no glyph, differs 11.4% purely because we draw the bevel and it does not. So this compares against a reviewed reference instead, and the tolerance is tight because our own output should be deterministic. The bevel being right is an argument from the spec, not a measurement, and it is one of the things the PowerPoint spot-check in ROADMAP.md should settle.

_scoreAs: `scoreAs` groups fixtures for the comparative benchmark (npm run compare), not for
the golden suite. Averaging text and structure together produces a number that says
nothing: on text-dominated fixtures every competent engine lands within a couple of
points of the others, because there the diff measures font rasterisation rather than
correctness. On structural fixtures the same metric spreads across a 40x range. They
are reported separately so the informative half is not buried under the floor.
`excluded` means the oracle cannot adjudicate the fixture at all; the reason is on
